title: Social Psychology · Episode 1
chapters: The spotlight effect: nobody's watching as closely as you think
Conformity: why we follow the crowd

units.t: Social Psychology. Episode one.
In this episode: First impressions, The spotlight effect: nobody's watching as closely as you think, Conformity: why we follow the crowd and Emotional contagion: how moods spread.
Part one. First impressions.
People judge your trustworthiness from your face in a tenth of a second.
Here's what drives snap judgements, and how accurate they are.
A tenth of a second.
In a 2006 study, Princeton researchers Janine Willis and Alexander Todorov showed people unfamiliar faces for just 100 milliseconds.
Their ratings of trustworthiness, likeability, attractiveness and competence were very similar to ratings made with no time limit.
More time mainly made people more confident, not different.
The amygdala, a brain region that detects threats, also responds to untrustworthy-looking faces when people aren't judging at all.

In a 2005 study, people shown pairs of faces of winning and losing US congressional candidates for about a second picked the one who looked more competent; that candidate had actually won about 70% of the time.
There is little evidence such faces make better politicians, so voters who know little may simply be swayed by appearance.
Halos and first words.
If someone is good-looking, we tend to assume they are also kinder, smarter and more competent.
This is the halo effect, named by Edward Thorndike in 1920 after army officers rated soldiers good in one respect as good in almost everything.
It works in reverse too, the 'horns effect'.
It shows up in job interviews, school marking and even courtrooms, which is why many employers use structured interviews and blind marking.
In 1946, Solomon Asch found that swapping one word in a trait list, 'warm' for 'cold', dramatically changed how people imagined someone.
In 1950, Harold Kelley's students expecting a 'rather warm' guest lecturer rated him more favourably.
What we hear before meeting someone can shape the impression before they speak.
Warmth and competence.
Susan Fiske and colleagues suggest we size people up on two dimensions: warmth, do they mean well towards me?
, and competence, can they act on it?.
Warmth is usually judged first, because intentions matter most for our safety.
Warm but less competent earns pity; competent but cold, envy; both, admiration.
You can't control your face, but you can control a lot.
A genuine smile, open posture, using people's names and real interest in the other person signal warmth quickly.
Clear, confident speech signals competence.
Be on time, match the setting's dress norms, make comfortable eye contact and put your phone away.
How accurate are snap judgements.
Some snap judgements hold up.
In 'thin-slicing' research by Nalini Ambady and Robert Rosenthal, strangers watching short silent clips of university teachers predicted end-of-semester student ratings surprisingly well.
People can also guess extraversion fairly accurately from brief encounters.
But face-based judgements of trustworthiness or competence often don't match reality, and they are heavily shaped by stereotypes about gender, race, age and attractiveness.
A 'baby face', with large eyes and a round face, tends to make people seem warmer and more naive, though it has nothing to do with character.
Different photos of the same person can also produce very different impressions.
First impressions stick.
Early information shapes how we interpret everything after it, the primacy effect.

In a classic finding by Solomon Asch, people told someone is 'intelligent, industrious, impulsive, critical, stubborn and envious' viewed them more positively than people given the same words in reverse order.
We then tend to notice information that confirms our view and explain away what doesn't, a form of confirmation bias.
Our impressions can even change how we treat people, which changes how they behave back, making the impression seem correct.
That's why it usually takes much more evidence to change an impression than to form one.
Notice your own snap judgement, ask what it's based on, and give people a second chance.
The first impression is a guess, not a verdict.
The key idea: We form impressions of faces in about a tenth of a second, and they can sway real decisions such as votes.
Part two. The spotlight effect: nobody's watching as closely as you think.
That embarrassing stumble, the stain on your shirt, the awkward thing you said: you're replaying it all night.
Everyone else has already forgotten.
The T-shirt experiment.
In a 2000 study, psychologist Thomas Gilovich and colleagues at Cornell University had students wear a T-shirt with a large picture of Barry Manilow, a singer then considered deeply uncool.
Each wearer walked briefly into a room of peers filling in questionnaires, then left.
Asked how many people had noticed the shirt, they guessed about half.
In reality, only about a quarter could say who was on it.
The researchers called this the spotlight effect: we believe we are noticed, for better or worse, far more than we really are.
Why we feel spotlit.
You are the one person you can never escape.
You feel every flush of embarrassment and replay every clumsy sentence in high definition.
When guessing what others see, you start from that inner view and adjust, but researchers argue we don't adjust nearly enough.
Everyone else is busy with their own spotlight.
Studies by Kenneth Savitsky, Nicholas Epley and Gilovich found people who committed a minor blunder in front of others expected harsher judgement than observers gave.
Observers see the wider context and remember their own slips.
While you rerun your blunder at 2 am, the witnesses have most likely moved on.
The illusion of transparency.
A close cousin is the illusion of transparency: believing our inner states show more than they do.
In late 1990s experiments, liars overestimated how many people would catch them, and people tasting a foul drink overestimated how obvious their disgust was.
A speaker may feel a pounding heart and wobbling voice and assume the audience sees terror.
Usually they see someone mildly nervous.
There is good news.
In a 2003 study by Savitsky and Gilovich, students told about this illusion felt less anxious and gave speeches that observers rated better than those of students who were simply reassured.
Knowing the bias breaks the loop of worry feeding worry.
The liking gap.
The same pattern shapes friendships.
In 2018, Erica Boothby, Gus Cooney and colleagues paired strangers for conversations, then asked each person how much they liked their partner and how much they thought their partner liked them.
Consistently, people underestimated how much they were liked.
The researchers called this the liking gap.
After a chat, we pick over our own awkward moments, while our partner was busy worrying about theirs.
The gap appeared in lab studies, among university students getting to know their housemates and in a workshop setting.
Many of us leave conversations more pessimistic than we should be, which can make us hesitate to follow up and build new friendships.
Turning down the spotlight.
The spotlight effect can keep us quiet in meetings or stop us trying a new dance class or wearing something different.
Knowing about it offers practical freedom.
Before turning down an opportunity because you fear looking foolish, remember the Barry Manilow shirt: far fewer people will notice than you imagine, and fewer still will care tomorrow.
When you replay a mistake, ask how much you remember of someone else's similar slip last week.
Probably very little.
After meeting someone new, assume they liked you more than your inner critic suggests, and consider sending that follow-up message.
The people around you are not your audience.
They are the stars of their own shows.
The key idea: People overestimate how much others notice them, a bias called the spotlight effect.
Part three. Conformity: why we follow the crowd.
Would you say a clearly shorter line was longer, just because everyone else did?
In a famous experiment, many people did.
The line experiment.
In the early 1950s, Solomon Asch asked American college students to judge which of three lines matched a reference line, a task so easy that people alone almost never erred.
But each participant sat in a group whose other members were secretly working with the experimenter, and on certain rounds they all gave the same wrong answer aloud.
About three-quarters of participants went along with the wrong answer at least once, and overall about a third of responses on those rounds matched the group.
Yet about a quarter never conformed at all.
Many who conformed later said they doubted their own eyes.
Why we conform.
Psychologists distinguish two pressures.
Normative influence is wanting to fit in and avoid rejection: we go along in public even when we privately disagree, as many of Asch's participants did.
Informational influence is believing the group has better information, especially in unfamiliar situations: if everyone is hurrying out of a building, you probably should too.
Both are often sensible.
Humans evolved in small groups where exclusion could be dangerous, and copying others is a fast, cheap way to learn what's safe and how to behave.
Brain imaging studies suggest that learning your opinion differs from the group's triggers activity in regions linked to detecting errors, so standing apart feels uncomfortable.
The details are still debated.
One ally changes everything.
In Asch's variations, when just one other person gave the correct answer, conformity fell to a small fraction of its usual level.
Even an ally who gave a different wrong answer broke the group's spell, because the participant was no longer alone.
Group size mattered only up to a point: conformity rose as the group grew to three or four people, then levelled off, so a crowd of fifteen wasn't much more persuasive than a handful.
Answering privately, in writing, also reduced conformity a great deal.
The lesson: a lone dissenting voice matters more than it seems.
Social proof and culture.
Marketers use social proof constantly: 'bestseller', star ratings, queues outside restaurants and laugh tracks on sitcoms.
In a well-known 2008 study, hotel guests reused towels more when a card said most guests in that room had done so.
Governments use the same idea, for example by telling people most others pay their tax on time.
It can spread good behaviour, but also fads, panic buying and misinformation, as the toilet paper rush in 2020 showed.

A 1996 review by Rod Bond and Peter Smith of over 130 Asch-style studies from 17 countries found higher conformity in collectivist cultures than in individualist ones like Australia, the United States or the UK.
Conformity in the US also appeared to have fallen since the 1950s.
Going against the crowd.
Conformity is not fixed.

In 1980, Stephen Perrin and Christopher Spencer repeated the line task with British science and engineering students and found almost no conformity, suggesting Asch's results were partly 'a child of its time', shaped by 1950s America.
Other repeats found conformity again, so context matters.
Most of the time, following norms keeps society running: queuing, driving on the left, keeping quiet in a library.
The danger comes when the group is mistaken or doing harm, and nobody wants to be first to say so.
In meetings, ask people to write down their views before any discussion, so early speakers don't sway the rest.
If you disagree, say so calmly and clearly.
You may be the ally someone else is waiting for.
The key idea: In Asch's experiment, about three-quarters of people went along with a group's clearly wrong answer at least once.
Part four. Emotional contagion: how moods spread.
One grumpy person can sour a whole meeting; one cheerful barista can lift a queue.
Emotions pass between people almost like a cold, and mostly without our noticing.
Catching feelings.
You walk into a tense room and feel your shoulders tighten before anyone speaks.
You chat with an excited friend and leave in a better mood.
Psychologists call this emotional contagion.
The term was popularised by Elaine Hatfield, John Cacioppo and Richard Rapson in their 1994 book Emotional Contagion.
It starts remarkably early.
In studies from the 1970s, newborn babies only a day or two old were more likely to cry when they heard another baby crying than when they heard other noises of the same loudness.
Long before we can talk, we are tuned in to the feelings of others.
Mimicry and feeling.
The main mechanism appears to be mimicry.
In conversation we copy each other's expressions, tone, speech rhythm and posture, mostly unaware.
Swedish psychologist Ulf Dimberg measured tiny electrical signals in facial muscles while people viewed faces.
Smiling faces triggered slight activity in smiling muscles, and angry faces in frowning muscles, within a fraction of a second, even when faces were flashed too briefly to be consciously seen.
Copying a face may nudge feeling through facial feedback.
A famous 1988 pen-in-teeth study claimed smilers found cartoons funnier, but a 2016 replication across 17 labs found no effect.
The 2022 Many Smiles project found that mimicking or posing a smile could make people feel slightly happier, though the pen method did not reliably work.
Facial feedback seems real, but modest.
Moods at work.
In a 2002 study, organisational psychologist Sigal Barsade of the Yale School of Management had volunteers negotiate how to share a pool of money.
Unknown to them, one member was a trained actor who behaved with cheerful enthusiasm, warm calm, irritable hostility or depressed sluggishness.
The actor's mood spread to the others, and groups with a cheerful actor reported more cooperation and less conflict.
Other research has found that leaders' moods are especially contagious, since people watch those in charge closely.
This matters in offices, hospital wards and building sites, where a calm supervisor can steady a tense shift.
Emotions are not just private states; they are part of a team's working conditions.
Networks and feeds.
In 2008 Nicholas Christakis and James Fowler analysed Framingham Heart Study data, which also recorded who was friends, neighbours or relatives.
They reported that happiness was linked among friends, friends' friends and even friends' friends' friends.
Critics noted that people befriend others like themselves and share environments such as suburb or job market, which can make happiness cluster without anything spreading.
The size of these network effects is still debated.
In a 2014 Facebook and Cornell study of about 689,000 users, news feeds were quietly tweaked for one week in 2012 to show fewer positive or fewer negative posts.
Users seeing fewer positive posts wrote slightly fewer positive words and more negative ones, and the reverse held too.
Effects were tiny, but contagion seemed possible through text alone.
The study sparked criticism because users had not knowingly agreed.
Guarding your climate.
Emotional contagion is not a flaw.
It helps us connect, empathise and coordinate.
But knowing about it gives you choices.
Notice when your mood shifts after time with certain people, places or feeds, and ask whether the feeling is yours or you have simply caught it.
People in caring and frontline roles, such as nurses, teachers, paramedics and police, are constantly exposed to others' distress and anger.
Deliberate decompression after a shift, through exercise, a chat with a trusted mate or time outdoors, can stop it piling up.
Contagion also works in your favour.
A calm voice can lower the temperature of a tense room, and spending time with steady, warm people is one of the simplest ways to borrow some of their steadiness.
The key idea: Emotional contagion is the automatic tendency to pick up others' emotions, and it begins in infancy.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What did Willis and Todorov find about judging faces?
Answer. Snap ratings closely matched ratings with no time limit.
Question two. In the Barry Manilow T-shirt study, how did the wearers' guesses compare with reality?
Answer. Wearers guessed about half noticed; about a quarter could say who was on it.
Question three. What happened in Asch's line experiment?
Answer. About three-quarters went along with the group at least once.
Question four. What did the studies of newborn babies show?
Answer. More often at another baby's cry than at other sounds.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
